alt: Six cards, one per global context, each with a plain-language summary. Orientation in space and time is highlighted as the context many Individuals and Societies inquiries use. Every unit has one global context, which shows why the inquiry matters.
caption: Six real-world angles; every unit uses one to show why it matters.

after: ## The six contexts, one at a time
alt: A table pairing each global context with the key concept and related concepts used in the guide’s example statement of inquiry, for example identities and relationships with systems, conflict and cooperation, and fairness and development with time, place and space, scale and disparity.
caption: Each context appears once in the guide’s examples, each with its own key and related concepts.

after: ## How a global context frames a unit
alt: A coastal city after a major flood sits at the centre. Four contexts each pose a different question: orientation in space and time asks how the response changed over decades; fairness and development asks which neighbourhoods were hit hardest; scientific and technical innovation asks whether defences reduced damage; globalization and sustainability asks how rising sea levels link the city to choices elsewhere.
caption: Changing the context changes the question, not the topic.

after: ## How a global context frames a unit
alt: Three cards for the Wall Street Crash, key concept change, related concepts causality and interdependence, and global context orientation in space and time, feed one sentence: a crisis in one economy can spread across borders and change ordinary lives for years. A statement that only fits 1929 is a fact; one that could guide a unit on another crisis passes.
caption: A good statement of inquiry links the concepts and context without naming the topic.

alt: The four year-5 strands of Criterion B: i research question and relevance, ii plan, iii gather information, iv evaluate. Strands i and iii are highlighted: the context justifies relevance and decides what kind of evidence is needed.
caption: The global context justifies the question in strand i and shapes the evidence in strand iii.

alt: A weak research question, is water access fair, is too broad. The better version compares piped-water access between two districts and asks what explains the gap. Its relevance is justified through fairness and development, and census tables and a short survey make it manageable.
caption: A focused question plus a context-based reason why it matters earns strand i.
